summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The three participants converged on a single execution contract for Recall, an offline-only iOS spaced-repetition app built with SwiftUI/SwiftData/Swift Charts and no network dependency of any kind. The contract locks in ten hard requirements (deck/card CRUD with fast keyboard-driven editing; a pure, injectable-clock SM-2 module gated behind a written spec with worked numeric examples before coding; a review session with per-card immediate persistence and no fabricated summaries for interrupted sessions; stats with 30-day forecast/history/retention and graceful empty/sparse handling; lossless CSV export/import with per-row error reporting for every malformed case; a recomputed, zero-suppressed daily local reminder; a reversible demo-data seeding toggle; centralized theming with full dark mode; and zero UI affordance for out-of-scope cloud/sync/marketplace features, each of which must instead be written up as a documented gap). Non-goals (cloud sync, accounts, push, community/shared decks, marketplace, media cards, sub-decks, ML scheduling) are locked. Production-readiness is defined as: compiles clean, SM-2 tests cover first-review/lapse/floor/day-boundary/DST/timezone-change via the injected clock, interruption-safety verified by an actual force-quit test, and every stats/import path has a verified empty/sparse case — with SM-2 correctness > review-flow speed > honest empty states as the fixed conflict tiebreaker for all later phases. Twenty numbered testable requirements were extracted covering every promise in the original prompt. One question was explicitly left open rather than silently resolved: whether demo-seeded decks count toward the user's real stats/streaks, deferred to the design phase.
open_risks: SM-2 spec-with-worked-examples could still be skipped or rushed in the design/build phase, reintroducing 'plausibly right' tests
DST/timezone-change test scenarios are easy to under-specify or omit in practice even though required here
CSV malformed-row enumeration may not be exhaustive once real-world file encodings are encountered
Demo-data vs. real-stats boundary is unresolved and could be implemented inconsistently if the design phase doesn't make an explicit, visible choice
Notification recompute-on-refresh relies on the app actually being foregrounded/backgrounded at useful intervals; a due-count could still go stale if the user doesn't open the app for days

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: All three participants converged in round 1 on a single research picture for Recall: the audience is self-directed, offline-first learners (language/exam/certification/professional drilling) who have likely already used Anki or Quizlet and specifically want zero-setup, zero-account, guaranteed-offline operation — a narrow niche rather than a mass-market play (explicitly ASSUMPTION-labeled, no external research performed). Comparable apps are Anki (trusted algorithm, rough/sync-oriented UI), Quizlet (polished but cloud/account-gated), and secondarily Memrise/Brainscape/RemNote (feature-heavy, configuration-dependent) — Recall's wedge is being a deterministic, provably-correct, zero-infrastructure 'reliable review engine' rather than competing on content discovery or social features. Platform-native opportunities identified: immediate per-card persistence, keyboard-first card entry, query-time calendar-day due computation, and calm explicit-state UI language. Five concrete risks were named beyond what the prior phase already flagged: SM-2 worked examples need cross-checking against a known external reference case (not just internal consistency) because this audience will notice scheduling that 'feels wrong'; the SwiftData schema for Deck/Card/ReviewLog should be frozen early since migrations risk silently corrupting review history; CSV test fixtures need at least one real-world exported file, not only hand-crafted edge cases; notification due-count staleness should be an accepted, documented limitation rather than something solved via unreliable background refresh; and the demo-data/real-stats boundary remains an explicitly open question for the design phase. The group agreed on build sequencing: SM-2 module and tests first as a standalone demoable unit, then frozen data models, then the interruption-safe review session, then stats, then CSV, then notifications last as the most cuttable feature, with CSV import (not export) being the first thing trimmed if time runs short.
open_risks: Demo-data vs. real-stats boundary is still unresolved and must be decided unambiguously in the design phase
SM-2 spec's external cross-check could still be skipped or done superficially under time pressure
SwiftData schema design in the next phase could still under-anticipate a needed future field, forcing an early migration despite the intent to freeze it
Real-world CSV fixture sourcing depends on someone actually obtaining a messy real-world file rather than only synthesizing one
Notification staleness is being accepted as a limitation, but users may still perceive it as a bug if not communicated clearly in-app

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: All three participants independently and unanimously concluded that Recall is a single-app project with no portfolio split required. The prompt specifies one named, deeply-scoped product (decks/cards, SM-2 scheduling, review session, stats, CSV import/export, local reminders) built around a single on-device SwiftData store and one due-card query — these are treated as inseparable organs of one coherent app, not independent services or sibling apps. The group explicitly rejected feature-aligned sibling splits (e.g., a separate CSV utility or stats companion app) on the grounds that they would either require duplicating the local database across apps or inventing a shared-data mechanism between siblings, which would itself violate the hard rule against faking infrastructure-dependent features. No portfolio-json manifest was produced, consistent with this being a single-app rather than portfolio-parent prompt. The selected app is recall-ios: an offline, deterministic, provably-correct SM-2 flashcard app targeting self-directed offline-first learners who've likely already used Anki or Quizlet.
open_risks: A later phase under scope or time pressure could be tempted to spin off a feature (e.g., CSV import, stats) into a separate 'companion' app to reduce build pressure, which this phase explicitly rules out and future phases must actively guard against

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: All three participants converged in round 1 on a single, precise product definition for Recall: an offline iOS flashcard app whose one-sentence promise is showing users exactly which cards are due today and never fabricating progress. The primary user is a self-directed offline-first learner (language/exam/certification/professional drilling, likely ex-Anki/Quizlet), with the defining UX scenario being a mid-review interruption (call, force-quit, OS kill) that must resolve with zero data loss. The core loop is locked as deck list -> pick deck or Study All -> review with reveal/grade and immediate per-card persistence -> session summary -> back to deck list, with stats, CSV import/export, and reminders positioned as satellite features reachable around, not embedded in, that loop. Hard scope boundaries reaffirm all prior non-goals (no cloud/accounts/push/community decks/marketplace/media cards/sub-decks/ML scheduling) and add one new one: no cross-deck merge/dedup and no auto-tagging or smart difficulty inference beyond SM-2's own output. The phase resolved an explicitly deferred open question from prompt_contract: demo-seeded decks are now specified to be visibly tagged everywhere they appear, excluded by default from aggregate/overall stats and streaks, viewable individually per-deck, and fully removable with no residue in real stats. Seven concrete, testable measurable success criteria were synthesized covering SM-2 correctness with external cross-check, interruption-safety, empty states across all six core screens, lossless real-fixture CSV round-trip, zero-due-day notification suppression, demo-data isolation, and a full airplane-mode run with no network-related crashes.
open_risks: The proposed three-tab IA (Study/Stats/Settings) was raised by only one participant and was deliberately not locked here — the design phase still needs to settle actual screen architecture

Demo-data isolation mechanics (tagging, exclusion from aggregates, clean removal) are specified in intent but not yet in SwiftData schema terms — the design phase must translate this into concrete model/query design without breaking the 'frozen schema early' constraint from product_research
The added non-goal (no auto-tagging/smart inference) could still be quietly reintroduced later as a 'small UX nicety' if not actively guarded against during design

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: All three participants converged on a concrete product brief for Recall. Target user: a daily, at-scale offline studier (300-3,000 atomic facts, likely ex-Anki/Quizlet) who values trust over features. Monetization is resolved concretely: Free includes the complete, fully-correct core loop (SM-2, review, CSV import/export, stats) forever, capped only at 3 decks/300 real cards and 30 days of stats history; Plus removes those caps and adds per-deck reminder customization, with a hard rule that a lapsed subscription never deletes or hides existing user data -- only blocks new creation beyond the caps. Core correctness and review-flow speed are explicitly walled off from any paywall, rejecting an alternative (speed/authoring-tool gating) that would have conflicted with the already-locked SM-2>speed>honesty priority order. Two build-critical details were locked: the App Store purchase transaction itself is documented as the sole, narrow exception to the offline-forever guarantee (StoreKit is an OS service; everything post-purchase works offline), and CSV import must surface plan-cap-blocked rows as their own distinct, visible error reason rather than folding them into malformed-row categories or silently truncating them. Competitive wedge (deterministic, provably-correct, zero-infrastructure reliability, no ads/dark patterns/paywalled correctness), growth mechanism (CSV file portability plus niche community presence, no accounts-based virality), and local-first/cloud-ready plan (SwiftData now, any future sync strictly additive with immutable history and deterministic conflict resolution) were all confirmed with no disagreement across participants.
open_risks: The specific free-tier caps (3 decks/300 cards/30-day stats window) were proposed by only one participant and not stress-tested against real usage patterns -- design/build phases should sanity-check these numbers don't feel punitive to the target daily-studier persona
CSV-import-vs-plan-cap UI treatment is specified in intent but not yet in concrete screen terms -- design phase must turn 'distinct visible reason' into an actual preview-row UI pattern
StoreKit offline-exception documentation depends on someone actually writing it into the gap/limitations doc and not just asserting it here

Cloud-ready extension path (encrypted mirror, immutable events, deterministic conflict policy) is a design intent, not a schema -- if the SwiftData schema isn't shaped with this in mind now, retrofitting it later could violate the 'freeze schema early' rule from product_research

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The three participants converged on a tightly-scoped validation slice for Recall: a fully correct, fully unit-tested SM-2 module (pure, injected clock, including at least one worked example cross-checked against a known external SM-2 reference) underlying a single-deck workflow where a user can add cards via a fast keyboard-driven form, run a complete review session with each grade persisted immediately to real SwiftData, and see a truthful summary only for a session that actually completed. The single defining validation interaction is a force-quit-mid-session test: on relaunch, every graded card must be off the due stack and every ungraded card must still be due, with zero data loss and no fabricated summary. Cut from this slice (deferred, not descoped from the eventual app): multi-deck management/archiving, CSV import/export, stats/charts, local reminders, and all monetization/subscription gating. Two corrections were made to the fallback model's proposal: the demo-data toggle is excluded from this slice as a real feature (only a throwaway internal seed path is allowed) since its isolation logic depends on aggregate stats that don't exist yet in this slice, and dark mode via semantic Theme.swift colors was reinstated as required at this scope since it is a global non-negotiable rule rather than a cuttable feature. Full DST/timezone-change SM-2 test coverage is sequenced into the later dedicated SM-2 build phase rather than required in this slice, though the day-boundary mechanism itself must be proven now via at least one concrete case. The phase explicitly frames its output as a validation slice feeding the already-locked build sequence, not a scope renegotiation.
open_risks: A one-deck, no-stats, no-CSV build may look thin if judged as a product rather than a validation slice — later phases must not mistake the cut list for a permanent scope reduction
The throwaway internal seed path used to avoid demoing against an empty deck could be mistaken for or accidentally evolve into the real demo-data toggle if not clearly separated in the build phase

Deferring full DST/timezone-change coverage to a later phase creates a risk it gets under-specified or skipped when that phase actually arrives, despite being explicitly required by DEC-prompt_contract-002

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase resolved several ambiguities that earlier phases had left implicit. SM-2 is now pinned to literal SuperMemo-2 arithmetic (EF'=EF+(0.1−(5−q)×(0.08+(5−q)×0.02)), EF floor 1.3, I(1)=1/I(2)=6/I(n)=round(I(n-1)×EF)) with an explicit grade-to-quality mapping (Again=2, Hard=3, Good=4, Easy=5) and a precise lapse definition (quality<3 only; Hard is a passing grade, not a lapse) — closing the risk that two builders would implement divergent, equally-defensible 'SM-2' schedulers. CSV format is now front/back/optional-note (three columns), resolving a contradiction where the locked lossless-round-trip requirement (DEC-prompt_contract-004) was incompatible with a strictly two-column importer given that notes exist on export. Due-date evaluation is confirmed to be a function of (instant, device's current timezone at query time), including the case where crossing timezones alone flips due status with no review taken — this and the OS-level iCloud-backup-divergence scenario across two devices are both to be named explicitly in the gap/limitations register rather than silently assumed. Per-card grade persistence must use an explicit synchronous save (not SwiftData's autosave) to fully close the interruption-safety guarantee, including a save-timed kill in the force-quit test matrix. The app's information architecture is locked to a 3-tab shell (Study, Stats, Settings & Tools). Additional edge cases were pinned down: CSV duplicate = exact case-sensitive front+back match with its own distinct per-row reason; archived decks/cards still count toward Free-tier caps; card deletion cascades to its ReviewLog (retroactively shifting retention stats, which is expected honest behavior, not a bug); grading buttons must not rely on color alone for accessibility; and daily reminder notification text must never leak card/deck content, only a count. One contributor (Gemini's local fallback) repeated its answer from the prior phase (next_steps_small) nearly verbatim rather than engaging with this phase's actual scope, and its contribution was set aside as non-substantive rather than treated as disagreement.
open_risks: The SM-2 formula/grade-mapping decision made here still needs to actually become a written spec with worked examples and an Anki cross-check in the dedicated SM-2 design phase, not just remain a decision-log entry

The three-column CSV format needs to be reflected consistently in the CSV design phase's schema and per-row error taxonomy without colliding with the already-locked malformed-row and plan-cap-blocked-row categories
Timezone-crossing due-status behavior and iCloud backup divergence both need concrete, discoverable in-app copy in the gap/limitations register during build, not just a decision that it should exist
Cascading ReviewLog deletion changing retention stats retroactively could read as a bug to reviewers/QA unless explicitly called out in test documentation and possibly UI copy

The recurring pattern of Gemini's local fallback re-answering a previous phase's question instead of the current one means future phases should not assume its contribution reflects the actual phase prompt without checking

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Gemini's CLI unavailable this round, Codex and Claude independently produced nearly identical MoSCoW breakdowns for Recall's full feature set, converging without real disagreement. Eleven must-have feature groups gate completion: the pure injected-clock literal-SuperMemo-2 scheduler with its full DST/timezone/lapse/floor/external-cross-check test matrix; deck/card CRUD with fast keyboard entry and cascading delete; the interruption-safe review session with explicit synchronous per-grade save and force-quit recovery at both mid-tap and mid-save kill points; per-deck and overall stats (30-day forecast, daily history, retention) with honest empty/sparse states; three-column CSV export/import with a full per-row error taxonomy and lossless round-trip tested against a real-world fixture; local reminders with zero-due suppression, count-only body text, and refresh-point recomputation; the demo-data toggle, visibly tagged everywhere and fully reversible with zero residue; centralized Theme.swift tokens with verified light/dark on every screen; a reviewer-visible gap/limitations register covering every documented non-goal and edge case; Free/Plus gating (3 decks/300 cards/30-day stats free forever, Plus removing caps and adding per-deck reminder-time customization, lapsed Plus never hiding data); and non-color-dependent grading controls. 3-tab IA and search/filter are should-haves (IA remains structurally locked from a prior phase regardless of this phase's should-have scoring); richer chart interactions are could-have; the full non-goals list (cloud/accounts/push/community-marketplace/media-cards/sub-decks/ML-scheduling/auto-tagging/cross-deck-dedupe/ads) is a hard won't-build boundary with zero UI affordance permitted. Two new concrete acceptance checks were added beyond restating prior decisions: CSV fixtures must include a real-world exported file, and hitting a Free-tier cap mid-review must not corrupt or block the in-progress session. Fifty-five numbered testable requirements were produced as the machine-readable adherence gate, 52 core (must-have) and 3 non-core (should/could).
open_risks: With only two of three participants substantively contributing this round, a genuine third independent perspective (Gemini's) never weighed in on this phase's scoring — future phases should watch for it becoming available and flag if it would have raised objections
The 55-item requirements-json is large enough that build/verification phases could quietly under-test a subset of it unless each is explicitly tracked against the adherence gate

Free-tier caps (3 decks/300 cards/30-day stats) remain unstressed against real usage patterns, as flagged in prior phases — this phase did not resolve that open risk, only reaffirmed the caps as designed
The should-have scoring of the already-locked 3-tab IA could be misread by a future phase as reopening the IA decision rather than being a build-priority nuance

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The design language for Recall is locked as 'The Honest Ledger': a calm, non-gamified, information-dense visual language (tabular numerals, ink/graphite palette with a single reserved amber accent for due-today badges and confirmed saves) chosen because this ex-Anki/Quizlet audience reads gamification as a trust red flag rather than an incentive. The default SwiftUI look (plain List/Form, system blue, color-only grade pills, generic charts, post-grade toast) is explicitly rejected with five concrete replacements, the sharpest being that no 'Saved!' toast may appear after a single grade since it visually implies session completion before the session has actually finished — confirmation is structural only (card leaves the due stack, counter decrements). The signature interaction is a fast (<200ms) no-bounce reveal-settle paired with four grade buttons rising from the bottom edge on an ascending shape/position/label staircase (not color-coded pills) with a distinct haptic weight per grade, satisfying both the review-speed priority and the already-locked non-color-dependent accessibility requirement for grading controls. Screens are fully inventoried across the locked 3-tab shell (Study: Deck List/Deck Detail/Card Editor/Review Session/Session Summary; Stats: Overview + per-deck drill-down; Settings & Tools: CSV export/import, Reminders, Demo Data, Plan/Subscription, and a first-class Gap & Limitations register screen), each with an explicit state model including two new substates — Deck List's 'all caught up' (has decks, nothing due, distinct from true empty) and Review Session's 'cap hit mid-session' rendered as a non-blocking inline notice rather than a modal, protecting the locked requirement that a cap hit must not corrupt or interrupt an in-progress session. Accessibility notes require Dynamic Type support without pushing grade buttons off-screen (card content scrolls, buttons reserved in the safe area), reduced-motion disabling the reveal animation while preserving haptics, and Swift Charts accessibility labels on all charts. Gemini's local fallback again did not engage with the phase's actual design-language brief and was set aside as non-substantive, continuing a pattern seen across prior phases.
open_risks: The palette and design tokens described here (ink/graphite + amber) still need to become an actual Theme.swift with concrete semantic color values in the build phase, not remain prose

The ascending-staircase grading layout and haptic ladder could still be cut as 'polish' under build-time pressure unless build/review explicitly treats them as the accessibility requirement's implementation, per DEC-design_discussion-006's constraint

The no-completion-toast rule needs enforcement during code review, since a well-intentioned engineer could add a subtle confirmation animation that still visually implies 'done' without technically being a toast
Sparse-vs-empty stats copy is specified as 'distinct' in intent but the actual microcopy still needs to be written during build
No independent third perspective has weighed in on visual/UX design across this or the prior phase, since Gemini's local fallback has now repeated a non-engagement pattern twice in a row

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The design_handoff phase produced a complete, numerically-specified DESIGN SPEC for Recall covering type scale (11 named roles mapped to Dynamic Type styles), a 4pt-based spacing grid, a full light/dark semantic color palette (15 roles including the single reserved amber accent for due-today badges and confirmed saves), corner radii, a merged canonical component inventory (with GradeStaircase, DemoDataTag, and InlineCapNotice flagged as non-regressable), the 3-tab/per-tab-NavigationStack navigation pattern with Review Session pushing (not sheeting) and hiding the tab bar, full per-screen state models with concrete copy for empty/loading/success/error/sparse/cap-hit states, motion (180ms critically-damped reveal spring) and a haptic ladder concretely resolved against iOS's actual 5 discrete impact-feedback styles (light/medium/heavy/heavy+pulse), and accessibility mechanisms (safeAreaInset-pinned grade buttons, explicit VoiceOver labels, chart accessibility summaries). Beyond pure visual design, this phase also locked architecture constraints needed to make the app's core trust claims actually hold: Review Session must snapshot due-card IDs into a frozen array rather than being driven by a live SwiftData @Query (which would let a mid-session grade reorder or shrink the visible queue), interruption-safety is implemented as 'recompute the due query fresh from truth on relaunch' rather than an explicit resume mechanism, the Deck/Card/ReviewLog SwiftData schema is finalized with Card.isDemo denormalized and ReviewLog strictly append-only, per-grade saves run synchronously on the main actor as an accepted small performance cost, and local reminders reschedule with repeats:false at four refresh points with a 'never created' (not merely 'stale') framing for skipped days. The decision was made not to run an external Claude Design pass by default, since the spec already contains every value a SwiftUI builder needs; a ready-to-use Claude Design prompt is preserved as an optional artifact only if the run is configured to pause for external design. Two of three participants (Codex, Claude) produced comprehensive, mutually-reinforcing specs differing only in exact hex/spacing values, which the coordinator canonicalized into one document; Gemini's local fallback again did not engage substantively with the phase brief and was set aside, continuing the pattern from every prior design-related phase.
open_risks: The GradeStaircase/DemoDataTag/InlineCapNotice 'must be their own file, do not regress' constraints depend on build-phase code review actually enforcing them, not just this document stating them

The snapshot-array Review Session architecture is a specific, non-obvious implementation requirement that a builder moving fast could still miss without an explicit test catching it (a Study-All multi-deck reordering test is recommended but not yet written)

ReviewLog append-only enforcement is stated as an architectural rule here but needs a concrete mechanism (e.g., no update API exposed) in the build phase to actually be enforced rather than just conventionally followed
The haptic ladder mapping (heavy + second light pulse for Easy) is a reasonable design given iOS's real primitives but has not been validated on a physical device yet, as required

No independent third perspective (Gemini) has substantively weighed in on visual/UX or architecture design across three consecutive phases now, which reduces the diversity of scrutiny this handoff has received

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase locked Recall's concrete iOS architecture ahead of tech_specs. The app is built as three layers: a pure domain Swift package (SM-2 engine + CSV parser, physically separated from SwiftUI/SwiftData with no direct Date()/Calendar.current calls), a thin SwiftData repository layer, and SwiftUI + @Observable presentation. The approved framework set is fixed to SwiftUI, SwiftData, Swift Charts, StoreKit 2, UserNotifications, UniformTypeIdentifiers, OSLog, Swift Testing, and XCUITest, with zero ML/AR frameworks and zero third-party dependencies (CSV parsing is hand-rolled). Beyond reaffirming prior architecture locks (snapshot-array review queue, synchronous per-grade save, frozen Deck/Card/ReviewLog schema), this phase added several concrete, previously-unnamed build-verification requirements: ModelContainer must have real error handling and a recovery screen instead of try!, with VersionedSchema/SchemaMigrationPlan scaffolding in place from v1; exactly one ModelContainer instance exists app-wide; the force-quit interruption test must be an automated, CI-runnable XCUITest using app.terminate() rather than a manual QA step; a Privacy Manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy) is required despite zero network calls; the notification permission prompt fires only on user-initiated Reminders opt-in, never at cold launch; StoreKit needs a checked-in .storekit config file with scripted expire/refund/renewal tests, privacy-policy/terms links on the paywall, and an explicit bounded error for offline purchase attempts; CSV import must use security-scoped resource access for document-picker files; and the Gap & Limitations screen needs its own automated test asserting required disclosure strings are present. Testing strategy is explicitly layered across unit, persistence, integration, and UI tests mapped to specific correctness guarantees. Codex and Claude converged with no real disagreement — Claude's contributions were additive risk-catches, not contradictions; Gemini's local fallback again produced only generic restatement and was set aside as non-substantive, continuing the pattern from every prior phase it has participated in.
open_risks: The physical Swift-package separation for SM-2/CSV needs to actually be set up as real separate package targets during build, not approximated as files in the main target under time pressure

ModelContainer error-recovery UI and migration scaffolding are architectural intent here but need concrete implementation and a test proving the recovery path actually works, not just crash-free happy-path testing

The automated force-quit XCUITest is specified as a requirement but depends on someone actually writing a CI-stable version of it, since timing an app.terminate() around an async save boundary can be flaky if not carefully constructed

Privacy Manifest requirements can shift with Apple's evolving policy; the required API-usage categories need to be checked against Apple's current list at actual submission time, not just this phase's understanding

No independent third perspective (Gemini) has substantively weighed in on architecture across any of the technical phases so far, consistent with the pattern noted in every design/architecture phase to date

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The tech_specs phase turned the architecture principles locked in ios_architecture_review into a concrete, buildable spec. Module layout is finalized as two local Swift packages (RecallScheduling, RecallCSV) for pure domain logic plus an app-target SwiftData repository layer and SwiftUI+@Observable presentation, with a full interfaces-json contract covering data models (Deck/Card/ReviewLog with per-deck reminder-override fields added), repositories, the review session pipeline, stats, reminders, subscriptions, and navigation. Two genuinely new technical decisions came out of this round: stats aggregation (30-day forecast, daily history, retention) is split into its own background StatsComputationActor (@ModelActor) reading off ModelContext.didSave notifications into an @Observable StatsCache, explicitly named as a separate concurrency domain from the main-actor synchronous grade-save write path so a future 'simplification' can't move stats math back onto the main thread; and the review session snapshot queue must gracefully skip (not crash on) a stale/missing card ID that goes missing between session start and grading, surfaced via a staleSkippedCount and covered by a dedicated required test — the Red Team catch this phase's rules mandated. Smaller concrete additions: typed per-tab route enums instead of a type-erased NavigationPath, a single injected PlanGate object as the one source of cap-counting truth across card editor/CSV import/deck creation, optional additive hardware-keyboard shortcuts for grading (layered on top of, never replacing, the locked tap-based/VoiceOver-labeled GradeStaircase), retentionRate modeled as an optional Double so 'no data' and 'zero retention' can never collapse into the same displayed value, and a fully enumerated CSVRowStatus type replacing prose description of the malformed/duplicate/cap-blocked-row taxonomy. As coordinator, one inconsistency between the two substantive contributions was resolved explicitly: Codex's interfaces used UUID as the canonical identifier while Claude's used SwiftData's PersistentIdentifier; UUID was chosen as the standing rule for all cross-lane contracts so PersistentIdentifier never leaks outside the SwiftData repository implementations. Named test suites (RecallSchedulingTests, RecallCSVTests, RecallPersistenceTests, RecallIntegrationTests, RecallUITests) now map directly onto the architecture layers, with the stale-ID skip and per-grade save-failure UI behavior added as newly required cases. Gemini's local fallback again produced only generic, much shallower coverage of the same brief with no new substance and no disagreement, and was set aside as non-substantive, continuing the pattern from every previous technical phase.
open_risks: The StatsComputationActor/StatsCache concurrency split is specified here but needs an actual integration test proving the didSave-triggered refresh path works and doesn't race with the main-actor write path, not just architectural intent
The stale-ID mid-session skip behavior is a new requirement with no existing test written yet — it needs to be authored during build, not assumed from this decision alone

The UUID-vs-PersistentIdentifier resolution requires every repository implementation to correctly translate between the two at the SwiftData boundary; a build lane that reaches for PersistentIdentifier directly in a view model would silently violate this decision

Keyboard-shortcut acceleration is additive and low-risk in principle, but still needs an explicit accessibility check during build to confirm it never becomes an implicit substitute for the staircase's VoiceOver labels

No independent third perspective (Gemini) has substantively engaged with any technical/architecture phase across the whole project so far, which remains a standing gap in scrutiny diversity noted since design_discussion

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: project_plan closed with a fully locked, dependency-ordered delivery plan for Recall. Sequence: parallel bootstrap of project/package scaffolding and the domain-engine milestone (SM-2 + CSV, reusing next_steps_small's validated code where it exists and passes its own tests rather than a wasteful rewrite, with the deferred DST/timezone/external-cross-check tests as the actual net-new work) -> persistence/repositories (with PlanGate introduced immediately as an unlimited stub to avoid the three-drifting-cap-counters anti-pattern) -> interruption-safe review session (cannot be marked done without both a genuine app.terminate() SIGKILL test, refined via a test-only post-save pause for timing determinism rather than a self-initiated exit, and the stale-ID mid-session skip test passing) -> stats (gated behind a spike proving the StatsComputationActor's cross-context didSave refresh actually works, plus a 3-second/3,000-card/3-year latency ceiling written into its definition of done) -> CSV workflows -> subscription/StoreKit -> final stabilization, including a Gap & Limitations disclosure that the haptic ladder is implemented per spec but likely unverified on physical hardware in this build environment. The single fallback/cut policy is locked to one tier only: CSV import trims first if time runs short (export stays), and no other must-have — including Free/Plus gating and cap enforcement — may be cut, since app_features already fixed those eleven groups as non-negotiable completion gates that no later phase may downgrade for scheduling convenience. Gemini's local fallback contributed a useful latency-ceiling NFR and the original flakiness-mitigation idea in round 1 but produced no substantive input in round 2 (a bare 'PASS'), continuing the shallow-fallback pattern seen throughout the project; its round-1 ideas were credited and incorporated, but it was set aside as a voice in the final resolution.
open_risks: The next_steps_small code-reuse path depends on that artifact actually existing and passing its own tests when task assignment checks — if it doesn't exist or doesn't conform cleanly to the frozen interfaces, the domain-engine milestone reverts to full-rewrite estimates with no buffer currently allocated for that discovery

The StatsComputationActor spike could still surface a deeper architectural problem than 'needs a retry loop,' in which case the stats milestone's estimate and possibly the actor-based design itself would need revisiting

The save-boundary test-only pause for the force-quit test needs to be implemented carefully enough that it doesn't itself mask a real save-timing bug — it must pause after the save completes, not around it

The haptic-hardware-unverified gap register entry depends on someone actually confirming no physical device was used by final stabilization and writing the disclosure, not just this decision asserting it should happen

The fixed single-tier cut policy assumes CSV import trimming alone is enough headroom if schedule pressure hits; if it isn't, this plan currently has no second lever to pull short of missing a ship date entirely

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: task_assignments closed with a fully locked, execution-ready backlog for Recall. Repo layout roots directly at the writable workspace with no nested recall-ios/ folder (confirmed against the actual session environment, where recall-ios is already the containing directory), using Recall.xcodeproj + fileSystemSynchronizedGroups so parallel lanes can add files without pbxproj conflicts. The four fixed lanes are cleanly assigned: data_domain owns the two pure Swift packages, SwiftData models, and repositories; services_utilities owns PlanGate, StatsComputationActor/StatsCache, ReminderScheduler, SubscriptionService, and DemoDataSeeder; primary_ui owns every screen, view model, and navigation route; polish_resilience owns Theme.swift, the three do-not-regress components, and — critically — the force-quit SIGKILL test, stale-ID/reorder tests, Gap & Limitations disclosure assertion, and final stabilization, kept deliberately separate from the feature-building lanes so the app's most safety-critical guarantees aren't graded by whoever is under the most delivery pressure. The backlog is 33 dependency-ordered tasks matching project_plan's locked sequencing (domain packages -> persistence -> review session -> stats -> CSV/reminders/subscription -> stabilization), each with owned files, checkable acceptance criteria, and requirement IDs in an R-<CATEGORY>-<NNN> scheme; reconciling those IDs against app_features' canonical 55-item requirements.json is deferred to a mechanical pass inside the final stabilization task rather than blocking this phase. Seven end-to-end user flows are declared covering deck/card creation, a full review session, stats viewing, CSV export, reminders, demo data, and the Gap & Limitations register, each using stable dotted accessibility identifiers for the UI-crawl gate. Gemini's local fallback again produced no substantive input across both rounds, continuing the pattern from every prior phase in this project.

The fileSystemSynchronizedGroups mitigation for pbxproj conflicts is a sound idea in principle but has not been validated against how this specific Xcode project will actually be bootstrapped by T-002's build worker

Both substantive contributors (Codex, Claude) converged after two rounds: (1) flows-json must gain a CSV import flow (select file -> per-row status preview -> confirm commit) alongside the existing export flow, since CSV import is one of six core features and the one with the densest correctness surface; (2) Recall/Services/GapRegisterEntry.swift's dual-writer risk (T-004 and T-030 both touching it) is resolved by making T-030 formally depend on T-004, with T-004 gaining an acceptance criterion that its skeleton must compile with placeholder entries; (3) the 'canonical 55-item requirements.json' cited since app_features does not actually exist as content anywhere in this project's history and must be authored and checked into the repo before T-001, with T-033's role downgraded from first-time authoring/reconciliation to a cheap mechanical diff against a real artifact; and (4) the locked Free/Plus split's second differentiator -- a 30-day stats-history window for Free users -- had no enforcing task in the 33-item backlog (only deck/card caps were wired via PlanGate) and must be added to T-020 (windowing parameter sourced from PlanGate.isPlus) and T-021 (visible windowed-history indicator, not silent truncation). A fifth addition, incremental build-verification checkpoints after T-011 (persistence + SM-2 tests green) and after T-018 (review session + interruption tests green) before downstream lanes proceed into stats/CSV/StoreKit work, was proposed by Claude, went unopposed, and is locked as a process rule with no change to task count, order, or lane ownership. Every other cross-phase consistency check (SM-2 formula/grade-mapping/lapse definition, three-column CSV format, PlanGate as sole cap-counting source, force-quit/stale-ID test ownership in polish_resilience, demo-data exclusion from aggregate stats, flattened repo layout) traced unbroken from its origin decision to the final backlog with no drift found. Gemini's local fallback again produced only a bare shallow pass across both rounds, continuing the pattern from every prior phase in this project.

The incremental-checkpoint process rule depends on whoever runs the build phase actually pausing and reporting at T-011 and T-018 rather than treating them as just two more line items in a 33-task list

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This second wave of write_tests closed the two most consequential remaining gaps from the first wave. Demo-data exclusion from stats is now real default behavior: ReviewLogEntry gained an isDemo field, RecallDataLayer.history(for:) populates it from the card's parent deck, and DemoSeedFilter's history/retention/streak helpers filter on it directly rather than requiring callers to pass explicit demo IDs, with matching coverage in StatsAndDemoFilterTests.swift. Far more critically, the project's single most important and longest-outstanding test — the automated force-quit interruption test — was built for real: ReviewSessionViewModel.grade() gained a #if DEBUG-gated pauseForInterruptionHook() that sleeps (only when RECALL_TEST_REVIEW_POST_GRADE_HOOK_MS is set) after the synchronous per-grade save returns and before the queue advances, exactly matching DEC-project_plan-007's timing requirement, paired with a genuine XCUIApplication.terminate() SIGKILL test in RecallUITests/ReviewSessionInterruptionTests.swift that grades one card, kills the app mid-hook, relaunches, and asserts the exact graded/ungraded card split. The integrator hand-verified both of these plus a CSV parser test correction (a blank CRLF line is legitimately absorbed as formatting noise by parseRows' finalizeLine(), not silently dropped data, confirmed by direct trace of the parser) and reconfirmed the prior iteration's Card(...) labeled-argument-order compile fix in RecallDataLayer.swift is still intact and unregressed. Separately, this is the ninth consecutive iteration in which Gemini's local fallback (and, this round, three other participants echoing its claim) narrated a fully-built ReminderScheduler service and test file that do not exist anywhere on disk — confirmed by direct file search — meaning local reminder notification scheduling remains entirely unimplemented (the UI only stores a time preference) despite repeated false completion reports, and this should not be treated as done by any later phase.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Build verification produced the project's first tool-backed evidence: a privileged external verifier ran xcodebuild against the iOS Simulator and confirmed a clean compile, independently corroborated by every sandboxed participant hitting the identical environment wall (unwritable clang module cache, dead CoreSimulatorService, failed swift-test stdlib load) when trying to reproduce it themselves. One minimal, verified repair landed: SM2TransitionResult in Packages/RecallScheduling/Sources/RecallScheduling/SM2Engine.swift gained wasLapse (grade.rawValue < 3) and dueDate (next.dueDate) computed properties, fixing a real compile error where SM2EngineTests.swift referenced properties that did not exist; the fix is semantically correct against the locked lapse definition and was the only file changed. The phase explicitly distinguishes 'compile verified' from 'test-suite verified' — no sandbox in this project has ever executed a full xcodebuild test/swift test run to completion, so all test-level correctness claims remain based on manual code tracing. Round 2 refined the standing gap list: the SM-2 'external cross-check and DST-transition test' item, previously bundled with the now-real timezone-crossing test, was split into two distinct still-missing items (a DST/non-24-hour-day test and an external-reference cross-check, e.g. against a known Anki-style interval progression), since a timezone-crossing test and a DST test exercise different failure modes even though startOfTomorrow's calendar-day arithmetic implementation is likely DST-safe by construction. Known product gaps (reminder notification scheduling, StoreKit/subscriptions, CSV export/import and Demo Data Settings UI wiring) were reconfirmed as real, file-search-verified absences and correctly left out of scope for this repair-only phase. The concrete next step agreed on is to point the privileged verifier at `swift test --package-path Packages/RecallScheduling` and `Packages/RecallCSV` specifically, since these don't require the broken CoreSimulatorService and are the cheapest path to this project's first real executed test pass/fail signal.

The SM2Engine.swift wasLapse/dueDate fix resolves a compile error but has not been confirmed by actual test execution to make the previously-failing SM2EngineTests assertions pass

Reminder notification scheduling, StoreKit/subscriptions, and CSV/Demo-Data Settings UI wiring remain entirely unimplemented in production code despite being locked must-have feature groups

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced a full manual simulator/device QA script for Recall, covering onboarding/launch, Study-tab empty/all-caught-up states, deck and keyboard-first card CRUD (including archive-still-counts-against-cap and cascade-delete-shifts-retention checks), the full review session (reveal/grade/staircase/haptics/session-summary-only-on-completion), Study All multi-deck behavior, Stats with distinct empty/sparse/populated substates and day-boundary/timezone checks, and a full accessibility pass (VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, Reduced Motion, grayscale-verified non-color-dependent grading, device-only haptic ladder). Every feature was explicitly classified as real-and-working, honest-placeholder, or fully-absent, and tested according to that classification rather than a uniform bar: CSV import/export and Demo Data are tested as honest placeholders (confirming their 'not yet available' copy doesn't imply function), Reminders is tested as a working preference-UI with an explicitly-absent scheduling backend, and Subscription/Plan is tested as confirmed-absent with no misleading disabled affordances. The most significant finding surfaced this phase: build verification's latest result shows RecallTests/ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift fails to compile on a main-actor-isolation error in a (plan:service:...) initializer, meaning the automated XCUIApplication.terminate() force-quit interruption test cannot currently execute at all — as a direct consequence, the checklist's manual force-quit procedure (grade one of two cards, force-quit within ~1 second, relaunch, assert the exact graded/ungraded split) is now the only currently-executable verification of the app's core trust claim and was written as an explicit numbered procedure rather than a one-line check. QA steps throughout were written in plain visual/behavioral language rather than referencing accessibility identifiers, so a human tester can run the script without needing implementation knowledge. Known gaps (reminder scheduling, CSV UI wiring, demo-data seeding, subscription/StoreKit, the broken test target, and missing SM-2 DST/external-cross-check tests) are documented as expected current state to prevent testers from misfiling them as new bugs.
open_risks: The RecallTests/ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift main-actor-isolation compile error blocks all automated test execution for the interruption-safety suite, not just one test — this needs a real code fix in a future phase, not just a manual QA workaround

The manual force-quit procedure is only as good as a human actually running it precisely (timing the kill within ~1 second of grading); unlike an automated XCUITest, there's no guarantee this gets re-run consistently as a regression check

Demo Data, CSV import/export, Reminders, and Subscription are all still gaps as of this phase; if any of them get real implementations in a future build, this checklist's placeholder-testing instructions for those sections become stale and need to be swapped for real functional tests
Haptic ladder validation still has not been confirmed on physical hardware anywhere in this project's history — this phase can only specify how to test it correctly, not confirm it has been
No independent third perspective (Gemini) weighed in on this phase's transcript, consistent with the pattern noted across nearly every phase in this project

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: app_store_readiness closed with a fully resolved launch plan for Recall's v1 submission. Positioning is locked to 'the flashcard app that never lies to you' — offline-first, no accounts, no ads, provably-correct SM-2, explicitly not marketing feature breadth. The app ships fully free with zero subscription/Plus/paywall UI or copy anywhere, since no StoreKit implementation exists after six-plus build waves; monetization is deferred to a v1.1 pass. Privacy label is Data Not Collected across every category, resting on PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy already matching the app's true zero-network, zero-analytics posture, pending direct confirmation it's present in the built artifact. The key resolution this phase reached was a two-tier launch-blocker framework, tested against the project's own fixed SM-2>speed>honesty tiebreaker: honest 'not yet available' placeholders (CSV export/import, Demo Data) are tracked gaps that do not block submission, since they openly disclose their own incompleteness — but Reminders, whose toggle/permission-request/time-picker UI looks fully functional while silently scheduling nothing (no ReminderScheduler exists), was judged a materially worse trust failure and a genuine blocker. After initially splitting on whether to fix or disclose Reminders, the group converged on removing its interactive UI entirely for v1 (replaced with a plain 'coming in a future update' line or folded into the Gap register), driven by the concrete track record that this exact feature has been falsely reported as complete across nine-plus prior build/test iterations without ever actually existing on disk — making 'build it in time for submission' a demonstrated risk rather than a hypothetical one, versus a near-zero-risk UI removal. Screenshot/storyboard assets and App Store description copy were updated to drop all reminders references to match. Final launch blockers requiring resolution before submission are: removing the Reminders UI, fixing the RecallTests/ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift main-actor-isolation compile error (so the interruption-safety claim has a real running test, not just hand-tracing), and adding a genuine support/contact URL both in App Store Connect metadata and as an in-app route — none of which currently exist. CSV/Demo-Data incompleteness and the absent StoreKit implementation are explicitly non-blocking, tracked gaps for this release.
open_risks: The three finalized launch blockers (Reminders UI removal, test compile fix, support URL) are decisions here, not yet applied to the actual codebase/assets — a future build phase must actually execute them, not just inherit the decision

Removing Reminders from v1 means this project's locked must-have feature list (which included local reminders) ships incomplete for v1 — this is a real, acknowledged scope reduction for the release, not just a documentation change, and should be tracked honestly as such rather than quietly forgotten
Deferring monetization to 'v1.1' carries the same standing risk flagged in round 1 — without an actual scheduled follow-up, 'ship free for now' has a real chance of becoming permanent
No independent third perspective (Gemini) weighed in on this phase across either round, consistent with the pattern across nearly the entire project

The support/contact URL requirement assumes a real destination (email or webpage) can actually be stood up before submission — this phase specifies the requirement but not the concrete URL/contact itself

Despite the genuine narrow fix, overall verdict stays NO-GO, unchanged in kind from three prior review cycles, because two explicitly-required checks were skipped again rather than performed: DEC-final_review-012's mandated direct grep of SettingsView/ReminderScheduler to resolve the Reminders live/dead contradiction was not done this cycle even though those files were readable in this exact workspace one iteration ago, making this a process miss rather than an environment gap; and DEC-final_review-011's study.deckCell_0 deck-creation-precondition question remains unresolved for a third consecutive cycle because docs/ui_crawl.json/docs/screenshots genuinely do not exist in this app_build workspace, a real environment limitation but one with zero progress toward external resolution. Prompt coverage is unchanged and materially reduced versus the original six-feature prompt: CSV import is export-only, Demo Data doesn't exist, Free/Plus monetization is deferred, and Reminders' true live/dead status is now unconfirmed rather than merely flagged.

No real executed test suite (xcodebuild test/swift test) has ever completed in this project's history; all 'compiles cleanly' and prior 'tests pass' claims remain source-trace or compile-only, never an executed green run, per the project's own standing DEC-final_review-002 distinction.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The portfolio_audit phase confirmed, with immediate agreement between both participants, that portfolio audit is not applicable to this run: Recall is a single-app project (one Xcode project, one app target 'Recall', two test targets RecallTests/RecallUITests, canonical source at /Users/pchordia/Documents/iOS-App-Factory/recall-ios/app_build), consistent with the portfolio_selection phase's earlier lock that this build has no sibling apps, no child prompts, and no portfolio-json manifest. Expected app count (1, recall-ios) matches actual project shape exactly, with no collapsed or orphaned categories — CSV, stats, and reminders were correctly treated as features of one app throughout the project's history rather than candidate sibling apps. The phase's main substantive contribution was a caution rather than a finding: this 'not applicable' structural confirmation must not be read as production-readiness sign-off, since final_review just issued a NO-GO verdict with three unconfirmed launch blockers and a non-compiling test target. summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase converged on a bounded, two-class fix plan for the seven failing UI-crawl flows and six dead-tap/back-nav reports from the release gate. Class 1 covers pure additive accessibility-identifier attachments (tab bar Label nodes for tabBar.studyTab/statsTab/settingsTab, index-based deck-cell identifiers, an actionIdentifier param on EmptyStateView, deckDetail.addCardButton on the empty-detail CTA, and card-editor front/back/note/save identifiers pulled from the real docs/ui_crawl.json step list rather than guessed) — all safe, no behavior change. Class 2 covers the five dead taps and one back-nav violation, which must each be individually traced to file/line and classified as either a real wiring fix (e.g. guarding StudyRootView's deck-editor save closure against a nil viewModel so the save button can't silently no-op) or an out-of-scope functional gap logged as a follow-up, never folded into one blanket 'fixed' claim. study.deckCell_0 is resolved by identifier only; if the review-session flow lacks a deck-creation precondition, that is reported honestly as a flow-definition gap rather than papered over with seeded fake data. The RecallTests/ReviewSessionViewModelTests.swift @MainActor compile fix is bundled per the already-locked prior decision. Scope stays strictly out of SM-2, persistence, CSV, reminders, StoreKit, and Stats. This room could not directly access the writable app_build workspace to verify file line numbers or the literal ui_crawl.json identifier strings, so that verification step is pushed as a hard gate onto whoever executes the fix.
open_risks: The full six-step identifier list for the keyboard-first editor flow was never actually read from docs/ui_crawl.json in this room — if the implementer guesses field names instead of reading the real file, the crawl can fail one step deeper on the next run, repeating this exact cycle's mistake.

If any of the seven flow failures turn out to be a regression of the tab-bar/deck-cell wiring DEC-final_review-004 already confirmed closed, that must be stated explicitly rather than silently re-fixed and re-claimed as new work.

Two or more of the five dead-tap reports may share one root cause (e.g. a single uninitialized-viewModel window affecting multiple Study-tab screens) — collapsing them into a single fix without saying so would overstate how many independent bugs were actually found and fixed.
No mechanism in this room can confirm the fix compiles or actually resolves the crawl until it's applied and the gate is re-run in the real workspace.
